subject: seasons
title: Why Do We Have Seasons?
summary: It's not about being close to the Sun. It's all about the tilt.

keys.answer: Earth's tilted axis. Different halves of Earth lean toward the Sun and get more direct sunlight at different times of year.

options.text: Earth getting closer to the Sun

keys.answer: It spreads out over a bigger area, like a tilted flashlight beam.

options.text: It spreads out over a bigger area

keys.prompt: In December it is winter in the U.S. What season is it in Australia?
keys.answer: Summer! Around December, the bottom half of Earth leans toward the Sun.

cards.title: A surprising fact
cards.text: Earth is closest to the Sun in January. But January is winter in the U.S.! So being closer to the Sun can't be why summer is hot. What is the real reason?

cards.question: What do you think causes summer and winter?

options.text: Earth getting closer to the Sun
Earth's tilt: which half leans toward the Sun

cards.reveal: It's the tilt! Around June, the top half of Earth leans toward the Sun. The Sun's rays hit it more directly, so it is summer there.

cards.title: Earth leans over
cards.text: Earth spins around an imaginary pole called its axis. That axis is not straight up and down. It is tilted, like a top leaning to one side.

cards.title: Leaning toward the Sun
cards.text: As Earth travels around the Sun, its tilt always points the same way in space. Around June, the top half of Earth leans toward the Sun. The Sun's rays hit it more directly, so it's summer there.
cards.example: Around December, the bottom half leans toward the Sun. Then it is summer in places like Australia and winter in the U.S.

why.q: Why does it matter that the tilt always points the same way in space?
why.a: As Earth goes around the Sun, first the top half and then the bottom half leans toward the Sun. That makes the seasons switch.

cards.title: Direct vs. slanted
cards.text: Shine a flashlight straight down on paper. You get a small, bright spot. Now tilt the flashlight. The light spreads out and gets weaker. Slanted sunlight is like that, so winter is colder.

cards.title: Why the tilt?
cards.text: Scientists think that long ago, something big named Theia smashed into the young Earth and knocked it off-kilter. Most scientists think the rubble from that crash became our Moon!

cards.prompt: In "Why Is the Sky Blue?" you learned that at sunset, sunlight travels through much more air. In winter, sunlight comes in slanted. What is alike?
cards.model: In both, the light reaches you at a slant instead of straight down, and that changes what you get: redder light at sunset, weaker light in winter.

cards.question: If Earth had no tilt at all, what do you think the seasons would be like?
nudges: Would summer and winter still happen?
Would every day be about the same?

options.why: Yes! Different parts of Earth get more direct sunlight at different times of year.

options.text: Earth getting closer to the Sun
options.why: Earth is closest to the Sun in January, during the U.S. winter.
The Moon does not cause seasons.

questions.q: In June, which half of Earth leans toward the Sun?

options.why: Right. That is why June is summer in the U.S.
The tilt always makes one half lean toward the Sun more.

options.text: It spreads out over a bigger area.
options.why: Yes, just like a tilted flashlight beam.
Color is not the reason. It is about spreading out.
Light speed is not the reason. The light is spread out.

sources.title: What Causes the Seasons?
sources.supports: Tilt, not distance, causes seasons; the tilted axis keeps pointing the same way; June and December; perihelion (91.4 million miles) in January and aphelion (94.5 million miles) in July; the Theia impact idea.

sources.title: Earth: Facts
sources.supports: Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees relative to its orbit, and this tilt causes the yearly cycle of seasons.
